article.title: Precision Fabrication
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A lot of people picture fabrication as someone cutting and welding metal to a drawing. That’s part of it, but the process involves several distinct stages before a single cut is ever made, and skipping or rushing any of them shows up in the finished product later. Interpreting the Design Intent A drawing communicates dimensions and tolerances. However, it doesn’t always capture the functional purpose behind a specific design choice. Understanding why a particular tolerance was specified changes how a fabricator approaches the manufacturing process. Austedan Fabrications and similar operations working on custom or complex jobs need to engage with this intent early, sometimes going back to the client or engineer with questions before manufacturing starts. Material Selection Against the Application The material specified on a drawing sometimes needs to be confirmed based on how the finished part will be used. A material choice that looks correct on paper can behave differently once you factor in the specific environment a part will operate in. We’re talking about corrosion exposure, temperature extremes, or vibration that wasn’t fully accounted for in the initial specification. This stage involves confirming grade and any required documentation before cutting begins. Discovering a material mismatch after fabrication has started is considerably more expensive to correct. Programming and Toolpath Planning for CNC Processes For parts produced using CNC cutting or machining, the programming stage translates the design into a specific sequence of tool movements. This phase determines the accuracy of the finished part and how efficiently it gets produced. Poor toolpath planning can introduce unnecessary stress into a workpiece. It also creates avoidable tolerance drift across multiple operations, or simply wastes material through inefficient nesting. Getting this stage right requires understanding both the CNC equipment’s specific capabilities and limitations. You also need to know how the part’s geometry interacts with the cutting or forming process. This is because the same design can be programmed depending on the sequence and approach chosen. Fabrication and In-Process Quality Checks The cutting or machining stage is where most people assume the real work happens. However, it’s rarely a single continuous process without checkpoints along the way. Measuring critical dimensions after key operations catches deviation early enough to correct it before it compounds across subsequent steps. This matters particularly on complex parts involving multiple operations, where a small error introduced early can shift and amplify through later steps if it isn’t caught until final inspection, by which point the part may need to be scrapped. Finishing Processes Surface finishing, whether that’s powder coating, galvanising, anodising, or simple deburring and edge treatment, affects more than appearance. Corrosion resistance, fatigue life, and how a part interacts with adjacent components during assembly all depend partly on finishing decisions made after the core fabrication is complete. Getting finishing specifications right, matching the coating or treatment to the part’s operating environment, protects the investment already made in accurate fabrication, since a precisely made part that corrodes prematurely or has a finish that interferes with assembly tolerances hasn’t delivered the value the precision fabrication process was meant to provide. Final Inspection and Documentation The last stage involves verifying the finished part against the original specification. It involves documenting critical measurements and providing certification or traceability records. This documentation matters particularly for parts going into safety-critical or heavily regulated applications. Proof of compliance is as important as the physical part itself.
